Open items (unclear, or a document we could not find) count as not met for the letter until a person checks them; the letter is then marked provisional. Results are given a known starting page for each hospital, from documents collected automatically. Letters: A 2, B 76, C 20, D 1, F 47. Status: graded 72, provisional 74.

Some documents were collected even though the hospital's site asks automated tools not to fetch them (robots.txt); this was a deliberate decision (Nov 12, 2026), and those hospitals are marked. Hospitals marked: 19.

Some pages and documents were collected with a headless web browser because plain downloads could not read them (pages built by JavaScript, or access checks a browser passes without a CAPTCHA). The browser names itself as automated and never solves a CAPTCHA; this was a deliberate decision (Nov 14, 2026), and those hospitals are marked. Hospitals marked: 7.

Documents agree with each other
Materials On Website
NO · not met
This hospital's documents contradict each other on at least one point.
9 points compared across the documents: 5 agree, 3 conflict; 1 not stated in two documents. Conflict on how to apply: “Submit or mail your completed application to: Attention: Financial Assistance Program, One Atwell Road, Cooperstown, NY 13326” (page 1) versus “Completed applications with all required documentation should be mailed to: A.O. Fox Memorial Hospital Financial Assistance Representative Business Office 1 Nor…” (page 4). Conflict on service area: “BHN will assume patients are eligible for financial assistance for residents of New York State, if they reside within the hospital’s primary service area of Cen…” (page 2) versus “Applicants must meet certain eligibility requirements and any Bassett Healthcare Network patient may apply regardless of the location of their residence.” (page 10). Conflict on contact details: “Bassett Medical Center (applications for O’Connor, Tri-Town and Bassett) 607-547-3480 800-642-0455” (page 4) versus “If assistance is needed with this application, please contact BHN’s financial counseling office at (607-547-3093).” (page 6). document
Rule: The law says a hospital's financial assistance policy must be clear and easy to understand. Documents that contradict each other are neither. This review checks that the policy, the summary and the application say the same thing on points such as who qualifies, deadlines and how to apply.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(c)
Model's reasoning

Consistency check: conflict on how_to_apply (b3aef8b3 p.1 vs 46e36a10 p.4); conflict on service_area (bdf455f2 p.2 vs 46e36a10 p.10); conflict on contact_details (46e36a10 p.4 vs bdf455f2 p.6); 5 point(s) agree. Model answered NO: A: relevant documents are the 2026 policy (bdf455f2), the 2025 plain-language summary (b3aef8b3), the 2026 application (3b5149e5), the financial assistance web page (848615a3), the PLS web page (1014b38c, links only), the emergency medical care policy page (127590f9), and the 2014 Patient Financial Assistance Guide (46e36a10) still linked from the financial assistance page. B: the current policy, summary and application agree with each other on income limit, FPL figures, discounts, immigration, timing and contact. However the out-of-date 2014 guide conflicts with current documents on service_area (it says patients may apply regardless of residence, versus the policy's town-limited primary service area residence rule), on contact_details (607-547-3480/800-642-0455 versus 607-547-3093) and on how_to_apply (per-facility mailing addresses versus one Cooperstown address). See consistency_points. At least one point is a conflict, so NO.

Service area drawn by the state's rules
Materials On Website
UNCLEAR · open: counted as not met until a person checks it
The hospital's documents did not let us decide this for certain. A person will check it by hand. Until then, the grade counts it as not met.
“BHN will assume patients are eligible for financial assistance for residents of New York State, if they reside within the hospital’s primary service area of Central New York (Little Falls, Delhi, Herkimer, Oneonta, Cobleskill, and Cooperstown, NY).” document page 2
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)
Model's reasoning

A: yes - the 2026 policy defines the PSA as 'Central New York (Little Falls, Delhi, Herkimer, Oneonta, Cobleskill, and Cooperstown, NY)' with a residence rule; the 2014 guide (46e36a10) instead says 'any Bassett Healthcare Network patient may apply regardless of the location of their residence.' B: the two documents do not give the same area; the policy (6/2/2026) is the most recent PSA definition and it is stated only in towns, not counties. C: the current PSA is not statewide or wider. D: the hospital's address is One Atwell Road, Cooperstown, NY 13326, but no document states which county Cooperstown is in (the guide lists an Otsego County DSS office but does not say the hospital is in it), so the hospital's county cannot be confirmed from the documents. E-G: cannot be checked - the PSA is given only as a list of towns and the rules say not to convert towns to counties myself; the DOH chart of assigned non-contiguous counties was also not provided. Per the reading rule for town-only PSAs, the answer is UNCLEAR.

No deadline to apply
Materials On Website
YES · met
This hospital's documents set no deadline for applying.
“Patients may apply for financial assistance at any point, including during the collections process.” document page 5
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(e)
Model's reasoning

A: no - no document states a deadline or window for submitting an application; the application says 'You can apply for financial assistance at any point during the collection process.' B: the only time periods found are the 180-day rule before collection referral, the 30-day determination window in the summary, and the policy's allowance to reapply every three months - none is a deadline to submit an application. The quote shows where this was checked.

No test of savings or property
Materials On Website
YES · met
We found no request for information about savings or other assets in this hospital's documents.
“Patient’s assets (such as house, car, etc.) may not be considered. Eligibility for financial assistance is determined solely on household income.” document page 3
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(e)
Model's reasoning

A: no document asks for asset information - the application requests only proof of income (paycheck stub, employer letter, Form 1040, benefit/award letters; dividend/interest statements document income, not account balances) and has no savings/asset fields. B: the policy states the opposite of an asset check, quoted here. The 2014 guide's mention of 'resources' and proof of 'interest and dividends' concerns county Income Assistance (Public Assistance) programs, not the hospital's financial assistance. All documents read; nothing counts or requests assets.

Service area drawn by the state's rules
Materials On Website
UNCLEAR · open: counted as not met until a person checks it
The hospital's documents did not let us decide this for certain. A person will check it by hand. Until then, the grade counts it as not met.
“BHN will assume patients are eligible for financial assistance for residents of New York State, if they reside within the hospital’s primary service area of Central New York (Little Falls, Delhi, Herkimer, Oneonta, Cobleskill, and Cooperstown, NY).” document page 2
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)
Model's reasoning

A: yes - the 2026 policy defines the PSA as 'Central New York (Little Falls, Delhi, Herkimer, Oneonta, Cobleskill, and Cooperstown, NY)' with a residence rule; the 2014 guide (46e36a10) instead says 'any Bassett Healthcare Network patient may apply regardless of the location of their residence.' B: the two documents do not give the same area; the policy (6/2/2026) is the most recent PSA definition and it is stated only in towns, not counties. C: the current PSA is not statewide or wider. D: the hospital's address is One Atwell Road, Cooperstown, NY 13326, but no document states which county Cooperstown is in (the guide lists an Otsego County DSS office but does not say the hospital is in it), so the hospital's county cannot be confirmed from the documents. E-G: cannot be checked - the PSA is given only as a list of towns and the rules say not to convert towns to counties myself; the DOH chart of assigned non-contiguous counties was also not provided. Per the reading rule for town-only PSAs, the answer is UNCLEAR.

Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. “Brooks-TLC Hospital provides financial assistance for medically necessary services to patients residing within its primary service area, which includes Chautauqua County and surrounding communities.” document page 1
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)

D: the hospital's address is 529 Central Ave, Dunkirk, NY 14048, but no document states which county Dunkirk is in. E: not a NYC hospital as far as the documents show. Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.

Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)

Service area drawn by the state's rules
Materials On Website
UNCLEAR · open: counted as not met until a person checks it
The hospital's documents did not let us decide this for certain. A person will check it by hand. Until then, the grade counts it as not met.
“BHN will assume patients are eligible for financial assistance for residents of New York State, if they reside within the hospital’s primary service area of Central New York (Little Falls, Delhi, Herkimer, Oneonta, Cobleskill, and Cooperstown, NY).” document page 2
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.

“For emergent and medically necessary health care services, a patient has to be a resident in The Guthrie Clinic Service area, which consists of the following counties: Broome, Bradford, Sullivan, Susquehanna, Tioga, and Wyoming in Pennsylvania and Chemung, Cortland, Schuyler, Steuben, Tioga, and Tompkins, in New York.” document page 5
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)

Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.

Service area drawn by the state's rules
Materials On Website
NO · not met

“Thompson Health also provides Financial Assistance to patients, who reside in our primary service areas, including Ontario, Wayne and Yates counties, and receive medically necessary inpatient or outpatient services that a physician, exercising prudent clinical judgment, would order or provide for a patient.” document page 1
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.

Service area drawn by the state's rules
Materials On Website
NO · not met
This hospital's service area, as its documents describe it, leaves out at least one county the state's rules require.
“Service Area includes ZIP codes in Orange, Sullivan, and Ulster Counties.” document page 2
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)
Model's reasoning

A: yes - the Financial Assistance Policy (b466cd10 p2) and the identical Billing and Collection Policy (a91f6ac7 p2) define the service area, and the policy (p2) and summary (83fac2cc p1) give a residence rule: New York State residents for emergency services, and patients who 'reside in Garnet Health’s primary service areas' (or work/visit there) for all other services. B: the policy/billing policy name ZIP codes in Orange, Sullivan and Ulster Counties with 'a primary focus on Orange County and Sullivan County'; the summary references the primary service area without naming counties. C: the area is not all of New York State for non-emergency care, so the county list is judged. D: the hospitals are at 707 E. Main St., Middletown, NY (Orange County) and 68 Harris-Bushville Rd., Harris, NY (Sullivan County); the web page confirms 'locations across Orange and Sullivan counties'. E: not a New York City hospital. F: the hospital's own counties (Orange, Sullivan) are named. G: but Orange County also borders Rockland, Dutchess and Putnam counties, and Sullivan County also borders Delaware County; none of these contiguous counties is included. The PSA therefore omits counties the 2007 rule requires (Rockland and Delaware with certainty; Dutchess and Putnam across the Hudson River). Answer NO. The DOH chart of assigned non-contiguous counties was not provided, so those were not checked.

Materials On Website
UNCLEAR · open: counted as not met until a person checks it
The hospital's documents did not let us decide this for certain. A person will check it by hand. Until then, the grade counts it as not met.
“For emergent and medically necessary health care services, a patient has to be a resident in The Guthrie Clinic Service area, which consists of the following counties: Broome, Bradford, Sullivan, Susquehanna, Tioga, and Wyoming in Pennsylvania and Chemung, Cortland, Schuyler, Steuben, Tioga, and Tompkins, in New York.” document page 5
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)
Model's reasoning

A: yes, the PSA is defined - the FY27 policy (p.5, above) and the FY23 NHSC application (p.2) each give a county list as the area whose residents can get assistance. B: both name, in Pennsylvania: Bradford, Sullivan, Susquehanna, Tioga, Wyoming; and in New York: Broome, Chemung, Cortland, Schuyler, Steuben, Tioga, Tompkins (the policy places Broome in its Pennsylvania clause, an apparent typo; the NHSC application adds a six-month residency rule). C: the area is not all of New York State and not the five NYC counties. D: I cannot tell from the documents which county the hospital is in - The Guthrie Clinic spans several hospitals in New York and Pennsylvania (Corning Hospital, Cortland Medical Center, Guthrie Lourdes Hospital, Robert Packer Hospital, Troy Community Hospital, RPH at Towanda Campus) and no document states any hospital's county; the only address given is a mailing address in Sayre, PA. E/F/G: because the home county cannot be determined from the documents, I cannot verify that the required contiguous counties are present; the counties named are reported in psa_counties for a person to check. The DOH chart of assigned non-contiguous counties was not provided and was not checked.

Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Rule: The law says a hospital's financial assistance policy must be clear and easy to understand. Documents that contradict each other are neither. This review checks that the policy, the summary and the application say the same thing on points such as who qualifies, deadlines and how to apply.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(c)
Model's reasoning

Consistency check: conflict on income_limit (698517cc p.1 vs 03c9c6a9 p.5); conflict on how_to_apply (03c9c6a9 p.8 vs 1a06f5a4 p.5); conflict on contact_details (03c9c6a9 p.11 vs cd7155e6 p.1); 6 point(s) agree. Model answered NO: A: Relevant documents compared: the policy (03c9c6a9), the application (1a06f5a4, plus the identical VD046 copy appended to the policy), the English plain-language summary (955829bf), the financial assistance program web page (a62737f0), the FAQ page (698517cc), the collection-policy page (817bd6d2), the contact page (cd7155e6) and Appendix A (ca59d676). The Haitian Creole documents (787ddb2c, a7f96150, c7171064) are translated copies and were answered from the English text. B: Conflicts found - (1) income_limit: the FAQ says assistance is for "household incomes less than the federal poverty level" while the policy, program page and summary say 500% of FPG; (2) contact_details: Mather Hospital's financial assistance office is listed at 75 North Country Road / 631-313-7712 in the policy but 100 Highlands Blvd Suite 302 / (631) 476-2801 on the contact page, the Melville unit at 2 Huntington Quadrangle Suite 4S01 is given phone 1-800-995-5727 in the policy/application/summary but (631) 313-7700 on the contact page, and the English summary prints Peconic Bay's zip as "110901" vs "11901" elsewhere; (3) how_to_apply: the policy requires a minimum of two pay stubs and three bank statements while the application lists one paycheck stub (or employer letter or tax return) as sufficient proof. Also noted: the application repeats the state form's "up to 400%" minimum while the policy promises assistance to 500%. See consistency_points.

No test of savings or property
Materials On Website
NO · not met
This hospital's documents ask about savings or other assets, for example bank statements, when deciding who gets help.
“Minimum of three most recent bank statements for savings and checking accounts” document page 8
Rule: Under the law, who qualifies depends on income: patients with income below 400% of the federal poverty level are presumed to qualify. The law sets no test of savings or property, and the state's application form does not ask about them. The application process must not be unduly burdensome.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(e)
Model's reasoning

A: yes - the policy's documentation list (Section E, p.8) asks for "Minimum of three most recent bank statements for savings and checking accounts"; the FAQ (698517cc) says "In some instances, you may be asked to provide your recent bank statements of general savings or any other asset-related documentation"; the program page (a62737f0) reserves "the right to request additional documentation related to resources for patients with household incomes under 150% of the federal poverty level." B: eligibility is described as based on Family Income, but requesting bank account statements and asset-related documentation is evidence of an asset check per the criterion. Answer NO.

UNCLEAR · open: counted as not met until a person checks it

“BHN will assume patients are eligible for financial assistance for residents of New York State, if they reside within the hospital’s primary service area of Central New York (Little Falls, Delhi, Herkimer, Oneonta, Cobleskill, and Cooperstown, NY).” document page 2
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)

Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.

Model's reasoning

Consistency check: conflict on assets (94e11b6a p.4 vs 94e11b6a p.4); conflict on time_to_apply (ba5919a3 p.3 vs 94e11b6a p.5); 6 point(s) agree. Model answered NO: A. Five relevant documents were compared: the policy (94e11b6a), the English plain-language summary web page (7aa18730), its Spanish translation (a946eaef, same content, used for languages only), the application (ba5919a3) and the 2026 eligibility-percentages sheet (cf1b5476). No separate physician-practice or faculty-group documents were found, so none were set aside. B. Two points conflict (see consistency_points): assets - the policy says liquid assets are not considered, yet its own medical-indigence section considers them and may require 'Information concerning available liquid assets'; time_to_apply - the policy's 30-day should-submit sentence conflicts with 'apply at any point/any time during the collection process' in the application, the summaries and the policy itself. Income limit, discount levels, immigration/residency, how to apply, service area and contact details agree; poverty figures are stated in only one document. Because at least one point conflicts, the answer is NO.

Service area drawn by the state's rules
Materials On Website
UNCLEAR · open: counted as not met until a person checks it
The hospital's documents did not let us decide this for certain. A person will check it by hand. Until then, the grade counts it as not met.
“Noyes also provides Financial Assistance to patients, who reside in our primary service areas, including Livingston and Steuben counties, and receive medically necessary inpatient or outpatient services that a physician, exercising prudent clinical judgment, would order or provide for a patient.” document page 1
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)
Model's reasoning

A: yes - the policy defines the PSA for non-emergency care as 'our primary service areas, including Livingston and Steuben counties'; emergency services are offered to New York State residents. The summary (ec7be49e) refers to 'the Hospital's primary service area' without defining it. B: named as the PSA: Livingston and Steuben counties (policy only). The Noyes web page lists DSS contacts for Livingston, Steuben, Allegany, Yates, Ontario and Wyoming counties, but as resources, not as the PSA. C: the PSA is not statewide for non-emergency care, so the county list is what is judged. D: no document gives Noyes's own address, city or county (the only address given is the UR Medicine Affiliate Billing Office at 73 Buffalo St, Canandaigua), so I cannot tell from the documents which county the hospital is in. E: the documents do not place the hospital in New York City. F and G: cannot be checked without knowing the hospital's county. The list is introduced by 'including', so it may not be exhaustive. Answer UNCLEAR and a person will check; the DOH chart of assigned non-contiguous counties was not provided, so those were not checked.

Service area drawn by the state's rules
Materials On Website
UNCLEAR · open: counted as not met until a person checks it
The hospital's documents did not let us decide this for certain. A person will check it by hand. Until then, the grade counts it as not met.
“BHN will assume patients are eligible for financial assistance for residents of New York State, if they reside within the hospital’s primary service area of Central New York (Little Falls, Delhi, Herkimer, Oneonta, Cobleskill, and Cooperstown, NY).” document page 2
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)
Model's reasoning

A: yes - the 2026 policy defines the PSA as 'Central New York (Little Falls, Delhi, Herkimer, Oneonta, Cobleskill, and Cooperstown, NY)' with a residence rule; the 2014 guide (46e36a10) instead says 'any Bassett Healthcare Network patient may apply regardless of the location of their residence.' B: the two documents do not give the same area; the policy (6/2/2026) is the most recent PSA definition and it is stated only in towns, not counties. C: the current PSA is not statewide or wider. D: the hospital's address is One Atwell Road, Cooperstown, NY 13326, but no document states which county Cooperstown is in (the guide lists an Otsego County DSS office but does not say the hospital is in it), so the hospital's county cannot be confirmed from the documents. E-G: cannot be checked - the PSA is given only as a list of towns and the rules say not to convert towns to counties myself; the DOH chart of assigned non-contiguous counties was also not provided. Per the reading rule for town-only PSAs, the answer is UNCLEAR.

“ensuring access to compassionate, comprehensive health and wellness for our North Country Community” document page 1
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)
Model's reasoning

A: no document defines a PSA. No document gives a list of counties, towns or zip codes as the area served, and none says residents of a named area can get assistance. The only geographic wording is the web page's general description 'our North Country Community' / 'River Communities', which is not a list and not a residence rule for assistance. B: nothing to list; the documents give no PSA, so there is nothing to judge against the 2007 guidelines. Answer NOT_FOUND.

Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.

Model answered NO: A: five relevant documents - the policy (e91a6e76), the plain-language summary (bfe0d429), the application (133f1f57), the discount percentages sheet (518a25ae) and the financial assistance web page (eaf44a66). No separate physician-practice documents were set aside; the 'Medical Group Visit' column in 518a25ae is part of the hospital's own discount sheet. B: see consistency_points - time_to_apply is a conflict: the application says 'You can apply for financial assistance at any point during the collection process' while the policy sets an Application Period ending 240 days after care and reserves the right to deny applications not received within it. All other points agree or could not be compared (poverty_figures, immigration_residency and service_area are stated in only one document each).

Service area drawn by the state's rules
Materials On Website
UNCLEAR · open: counted as not met until a person checks it
The hospital's documents did not let us decide this for certain. A person will check it by hand. Until then, the grade counts it as not met.
“Patients may qualify for financial assistance for emergency services if they are a resident of New York State and for all other services if they reside within the hospitals primary service area which includes Cayuga, Chemung, Cortland, Schuyler, Tioga, Steuben, Thompkins, and Northern Tioga, PA.” document page 1
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)
Model's reasoning

A: yes - the policy (p1) and the summary (p1) both define the PSA as a residence rule: emergency services for New York State residents, all other services for residents of the listed counties. B: both documents name the identical list: Cayuga, Chemung, Cortland, Schuyler, Tioga, Steuben, 'Thompkins' (Tompkins), and Northern Tioga, PA. C: the non-emergency area is not statewide, so the county list must be judged. D: the documents place Arnot Health's campuses 'in Elmira' and 'in Bath, NY' (web page; application address 600 Roe Ave, Elmira, NY 14905) but never state what county the hospital is in, so the hospital's county cannot be confirmed from the documents. E: not a New York City hospital. F/G: because the documents do not name the hospital's county, I cannot confirm from the documents alone that the list contains the hospital's own county and every county bordering it; I will not substitute outside geographic knowledge. The DOH chart of assigned non-contiguous counties was not provided and was not checked. A person should verify whether the hospital's county (and all counties bordering it) is on the list.

Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. “The service area includes all counties contiguous to a UPMC facility.” document page 1
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)
Model's reasoning

A: yes - the financial services web page gives a residence rule for non-emergency assistance: 'Live in the primary service area of a UPMC provider' and 'The service area includes all counties contiguous to a UPMC facility.' B: that description is the only PSA definition; it names no counties, and no other applicable document defines it. C: it does not cover all of New York State or the five NYC counties. D: the hospital's own county cannot be told from the documents - the hospital is named 'UPMC Chautauqua' but no address, city or county is given for it anywhere. E/F/G: because the PSA is stated only as a description (counties contiguous to a UPMC facility) rather than a named state, city or county list, and the hospital's county is not stated, I cannot verify that the hospital's own county and all bordering counties are included; the definition also arguably omits the facility's own county. Answer UNCLEAR per the reading rules; the DOH chart of assigned non-contiguous counties was not checked.

Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. “provides discounts to qualifying individuals based on their income and who reside within our Primary Service Area (PSA)” document page 1
Rule: The law says a hospital must give financial assistance for necessary, non-emergency care to patients who live in its "primary service area", and that the State Health Commissioner sets the rules for drawing that area. Under the state's 2007 rules, the area must include at least the hospital's own county and every county that borders it; for a New York City hospital, all five boroughs and the counties that border them. A hospital may not draw its area to leave out poorer or uninsured communities.
N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2807-k(9-a)(f)(i)
Model's reasoning

Per the reading rules, referring to an undefined 'primary service area' does not define it, so there is no definition to judge; checks B-G are not reached. (The documents show the hospital is at 785 Mamaroneck Avenue, White Plains, NY.) No counties are named anywhere, so the psa_counties list is empty.
